en: Zulpukor cannot pierce; draw back.
The decree of the One God, Jappar,
Will be thus; behold it.
Your ribs will crack and split;
Your blood will be spilled in this place.
Better than that, Khan Manas,
Reach Talas and die there!'
When he led his troops and turned back,
Your leopard father, your protecting spirit,
When he turned back in mourning,
In Chatkal of vast Beijing,
In the marshes of the clear water,
Your father Manas the leopard,
When he dipped his hands into the water,
When he performed his ablution,
In the fortress of Beijing,
When the afternoon prayer time came,
When he turned his face northward,
When your father stood reciting his prayer,
Azhybai of the Argyn khan,
Six bowshots behind,
That guard, the Argyn khan's son,
Had let his eyes fall asleep.
With a cotton belt and broad boots,
The warrior Kalcha, khan of the monks,
Konurbai, mighty in cunning,
Had stalked your father and reached him.
Let me tell the rest:
Having spread his prayer mat,
Through the ridge of his back,
Your father, Khan Manas,
Was stabbed, his lung pierced through.
Azhybai of the Argyn khan,
Unable to hold still for fright,
Turned Kartkuron's head
And thrust his spear at Kalcha.
A blue-mottled star in the sky was eclipsed;
Konurbai, whose horse was swift,
Fled in plain sight and escaped.
The spear was left in the back;
Flustered and hurrying, Akybai
Twisted and pulled the spear out.
The steel point cracked
And broke off in the backbone.
My warrior did not speak of his wound
And thus brought this wretched woman misery.
Had I been a man instead of a woman,
My darling orphan,
Had I been your father's watchman,
Had I been the warrior Azhybai,
Would I not have marked out my resolve!
With his cotton belt and broad boots,
That swine, the monks' khan,
Would I not have shown him some sport!
Would I not have tested the swift horse,
Stabbing that rotten wretch from behind,
Would I not have made Beijing endure
A spectacle of slaughter and upheaval!
Your father kept it unspoken,
Digging my pit deep,
Boiling misery for me.
The spear point left within him
Had shown your father a terrible spectacle.
Your father coughed in sharp bursts,
Lifting his head from the pillow.
When he raised his head and cried 'Ah!'
Bowlful after bowlful of blood came out.
Unable to collect myself,
I, the unfortunate one, lost my strength.
He coughed and coughed,
Lifting his head with a rattle.
When your father rasped out 'Ah!'
Shovelful after shovelful of blood came out.
Twelve pits filled to the brim,
And I, your unfortunate mother, lost my strength.
As blood left him, strength left him,
And death came upon your father.
Smoothing his fine moustache,
His soul drawing toward Judgment,
His wide eyes closed,
And he faded toward the hereafter.
He opened his eyes and spoke:
'Alas, my lady!' he said.
'When the khan dies, to his wife
Her birth family is near,' he said.
'This Talas is no land for you;
My lady, these Kyrgyz are no people of yours.
To Temir Khan's city
Go as a wanderer and make your living.
Of the little one gained through mortal hardship,
Cut his twig;
Perform his rite.
Have an amulet hung about his neck;
Have your brother Ismail rear him.
When he reaches twelve,
Show him Talas again.
If my spirit is still present,
I shall meet him on his road,' he said.
That was the promise your father the khan made.
Go and see: that is the place Ken-Shor.
I am the one who swallowed your father Manas!
Left behind at his head,
I devoured your father the khan
At the age of thirty-two.
When your father Manas died,
When he went to the other world,
Alas for this world!
'My precious one, take me with you!' they cried.
The forty companions left by your father
Stood in a row and wailed.
A dark forest of willows grew;
God had become your father's friend.
Throughout this Ken-Shor,
My orphan foal, go and see,
When your valiant father died,
'My warrior, take me with you!' I cried,
My black hair untouched by a comb,
I then tore out strand by strand.
Where I tore out my hair strand by strand,
Willow after willow grew into a forest;
The holy protectors became your father's friends.
Here today in Ken-Shor,
My orphan foal, go and see:
The dark blood that flowed from my face
Became red stone a horse's shin deep.
Your father the khan became the people's head.
The dark tears that flowed from my eyes
Throughout this Ken-Shor
Became pools of clear water.
Your father became a banner to the people.
He twisted and curled his moustache;
The prophets supported your father.
He twisted and curled his beard;
The Companions supported your father.
When your father Manas died,
Koshoi and Khan Toshtuk wept;
Everyone who had met your father wept.
On the hills, the horses had pied heads;
Sixty calamities came at once;
Behind him, his son was still a child.
My rib bones were torn apart,
The tears poured from my eyes,
And my heart was sorely divided.
Allah's sun grew overcast in the sky;
Sixty afflictions came upon my head at once.
'If I bury the generous hero openly,
Will the enemy dig him up?
Dragging him onto the road,
Will they tear him apart for the great dogs?
Will they take their vengeance thus?'
I, your unfortunate mother,
Made my towering head a banner,
Made a warrior of my woman's self.
To hide the blood-shedding hero,
I raised an outcry among the people.
I made ready five executioners;
I used Zhelmayan for labor.
I had vast Egypt searched;
Of people who did not know our tongue,
I had eighty Arabs brought.
Without letting one person know,
Without letting anyone suspect,
Giving horses as payment,
I, the unfortunate one, spared nothing;
I scattered my treasury and gave at once.
I gave sharp iron crowbars,
Gave steel hoes and possessions,
In Kara-Too of Ichkilik,
A huge cliff standing still,
On this side of Talas,
On this edge of Ken-Kol,
I had the dark cliff's side hollowed out.
I opened its mouth, poor soul,
Wide enough for only one person;
I had the space beyond hollowed out
Wide enough for six thousand sheep to lie.
'The roof may fall,' I thought,
'It may bring me down in this way,' I thought.
'If the black earth covers the generous hero,
He will decay needlessly,' I thought.
Sparing none of my empty worldly wealth,
I had pillars fashioned of gold.
At sixty points,
I had pillars of gold set up.
My precious orphan, listen
To how I buried your father!
'It may grow foul inside,' I thought;
I showed my skill.
The clear water above,
I had a channel broken for it with iron crowbars
And led it through the cave.
Again, orphan, listen:
I had ruby stone split;
In sixty different places,
Rubies mingled with precious gems
I had made into lamps.
'The underside may decay,' I thought,
And forged a bed of gold.
My foal, this labor of mine was beyond measure.
With the holy Quran as his pillow,
Upon the bed,
With his head toward the qibla,
'For one clothed in fine white cloth, there is no questioning';
I laid bedding of that fine cloth.
All around it, with precious gems,
I had the space spread and covered.
'He may decay,' I thought;
In his resting place
I had juniper ashes scattered.
When his resting place was complete,
To my close ones, Koshoi and Toshtuk,
I told my secret as faithfully as my creed;
To my leopard uncle Bakai,
I told the truth.
Koshoi and Bakai, pouring out their feelings,
Implored your mother:
'O Kanykei, my foal,
May whoever calls you a mere woman fail to prosper!
Whoever calls you a female,
May none of his undertakings ever thrive!'
I had vast Mecca searched;
The great imam of Mecca,
The White Ishan, I had brought.
I had a horse of honor saddled;
I had the funeral prayer recited.
I had his shroud cut and bound;
Bakai and the warrior Koshoi,
These two I had wash him.
All the mighty men gathered;
At the place where they took him for the funeral prayer,
Plane trees and poplars grew.
God truly supported your father.
As dusk came and the sun set,
As the first of the people lay still,
I had the champions carry him
And held a lantern before him.
No mortal knew the cave.
With you, orphan, beneath my arm,
I myself hurried there.
Carrying your father's body,
The forty ishans recited the confession of faith.
All the way to that cave,
Red willow shoots sprang up;
God became your father's friend.
When I went to the cave,
Foolish people were afraid.
Koshoi, Toshtuk and Kokboru
Recited the Quran together.
When your father entered his resting place,
Koshoi and the elder Toshtuk—
Their khan entered the cave.
All the people who had gone there
Entered the cave as well.
With the forty ishans at their head,
They fitted inside with room to spare.
